question: The traditional zoning approach of separating a jurisdiction into distinct districts (residential, commercial, industrial, etc.) with use restrictions specific to each district, upheld by the U.S. Supreme Court in Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty Co. (1926), is known as:
choice_a: Euclidean zoning
choice_b: Performance zoning
choice_c: Incentive zoning
explanation: Euclidean zoning -- named for the landmark 1926 U.S. Supreme Court case Village of Euclid, Ohio v. Ambler Realty Co., which upheld the constitutionality of comprehensive municipal zoning -- refers to traditional use-based zoning that divides a jurisdiction into separate districts (residential, commercial, industrial, agricultural) with distinct permitted uses and dimensional standards for each district.
source_note: Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty Co., 272 U.S. 365 (1926); standard national zoning law history, well-corroborated

question: A use that is not automatically permitted within a zoning district but may be allowed after review and approval by the local zoning board upon a showing that it meets specified standards and will not harm the surrounding area (e.g., a church or daycare in a residential district) is called a:
choice_a: Special exception (conditional use)
choice_b: Variance
choice_c: Legal nonconforming use
explanation: A special exception, also called a conditional use, is a use expressly contemplated by the zoning ordinance as potentially compatible with a district but requiring case-by-case discretionary approval based on defined criteria -- unlike a variance, which excuses a property from a specific dimensional or use requirement due to hardship, not because the use itself was anticipated by the ordinance.
source_note: Standard national zoning law terminology -- special exception/conditional use, well-corroborated; distinguished from variance already covered elsewhere in this bank

question: A local government rezones a single small parcel to a classification that is inconsistent with the surrounding area and the comprehensive plan, singling it out for treatment different from neighboring, similarly situated land, primarily to benefit (or burden) that one owner. This is most likely to be challenged as illegal:
choice_a: Spot zoning
choice_b: A valid text amendment to the land development code
choice_c: A legitimate comprehensive plan update
explanation: Spot zoning occurs when a small parcel is singled out for a use classification inconsistent with the surrounding area and the comprehensive plan, primarily for the benefit of a particular owner rather than in furtherance of a comprehensive, community-wide land use scheme; because it lacks the required consistency with the comprehensive plan, spot zoning is generally invalid and subject to legal challenge.
source_note: Standard national zoning law doctrine -- spot zoning, well-corroborated

question: The government's constitutional power to take private property for a public use, provided the owner receives just compensation, is known as:
choice_a: Eminent domain
choice_b: Escheat
choice_c: Police power
explanation: Eminent domain is the inherent power of government (or certain authorized private entities such as utilities) to take private property for a public use upon payment of just compensation to the owner, as required by the Fifth Amendment's Takings Clause and the corresponding provision of the Florida Constitution.
source_note: U.S. Const. amend. V; Fla. Const. art. X, Section 6(a); standard real estate law terminology, well-corroborated

question: A property owner believes a government regulation has so severely restricted the use of her land that it amounts to a taking, even though the government never filed a formal condemnation action or took title. The legal action she would bring to seek compensation is called:
choice_a: Inverse condemnation
choice_b: Quiet title action
choice_c: Partition action
explanation: Inverse condemnation is a lawsuit brought by a property owner (rather than the government) alleging that a governmental action or regulation has effectively taken the property, or a significant property interest, without formal exercise of eminent domain or payment of compensation -- the owner must initiate the case and prove a compensable taking occurred.
source_note: Standard national land use/takings law terminology -- inverse condemnation, well-corroborated

question: In Lucas v. South Carolina Coastal Council, the U.S. Supreme Court held that a land use regulation that deprives an owner of essentially all economically viable use of the property generally constitutes:
choice_a: A regulatory taking requiring just compensation, unless the restriction reflects background principles of state property or nuisance law
choice_b: A valid exercise of police power that never requires compensation, regardless of the regulation's economic effect
choice_c: A criminal violation of the property owner's due process rights
choice_d: An automatic entitlement to rezoning of the property
explanation: In Lucas v. South Carolina Coastal Council (1992), the Supreme Court held that a regulation denying a landowner all economically beneficial or productive use of land is a categorical (per se) taking requiring compensation, unless the state can show the prohibited use was never part of the owner's title to begin with under background principles of nuisance or property law.
source_note: Lucas v. South Carolina Coastal Council, 505 U.S. 1003 (1992); standard national land use/takings law, well-corroborated

question: Under Penn Central Transportation Co. v. City of New York, when a land use regulation restricts but does not eliminate all economic use of a property, courts weigh factors such as the regulation's economic impact, its interference with investment-backed expectations, and the character of the government action to determine whether:
choice_a: A compensable partial regulatory taking has occurred
choice_b: The property qualifies for a homestead exemption
choice_c: The owner may automatically demand a rezoning to the highest and best use
choice_d: The property is exempt from all future taxation
explanation: Penn Central Transportation Co. v. City of New York (1978) established the ad hoc balancing test used for partial (non-categorical) regulatory takings claims, weighing the economic impact of the regulation, the extent of interference with distinct investment-backed expectations, and the character of the governmental action -- a fact-specific inquiry distinct from the categorical rule for total takings.
source_note: Penn Central Transportation Co. v. City of New York, 438 U.S. 104 (1978); standard national land use/takings law, well-corroborated

question: Responding to the U.S. Supreme Court's Kelo v. City of New London decision, which broadly interpreted 'public use' to include economic development, the Florida Legislature and voters in 2006 amended state law and the Florida Constitution to:
choice_a: Prohibit the use of eminent domain to transfer property from one private owner to another primarily for private economic development
choice_b: Expand local governments' eminent domain power to include any private commercial redevelopment project
choice_c: Abolish eminent domain entirely in Florida
choice_d: Eliminate the requirement to pay just compensation in condemnation cases
explanation: In direct response to Kelo v. City of New London (2005), Florida enacted Section 73.013, F.S., restricting eminent domain to traditional public purposes and barring its use to transfer condemned property to another private owner for economic development, and voters approved a 2006 constitutional amendment (requiring a three-fifths legislative vote for exceptions) reinforcing that restriction.
source_note: Section 73.013, F.S.; Fla. Const. art. X, Section 6(c); Kelo v. City of New London, 545 U.S. 469 (2005)

question: A zoning technique that permits a mix of residential, commercial, and open-space uses within a single large development under one master site plan, generally offering more design flexibility than conventional Euclidean zoning in exchange for greater upfront regulatory review, is known as a:
choice_a: Planned Unit Development (PUD)
choice_b: Legal nonconforming use
choice_c: Variance
explanation: A Planned Unit Development (PUD) is a zoning technique that allows a developer to plan a mixed-use or unified development (combining residential, commercial, and/or open space) under a single master plan, typically offering flexibility from conventional lot-by-lot zoning standards in exchange for more detailed upfront site plan review and often enhanced amenities or open space.
source_note: Standard national zoning law terminology -- PUD, well-corroborated

question: A zoning tool that superimposes additional requirements or protections on top of an existing base zoning district -- for example, adding historic preservation or airport-noise restrictions across several districts -- without changing the underlying base zoning classification, is called a(n):
choice_a: Overlay zoning district
choice_b: Special exception
choice_c: Nonconforming use
explanation: An overlay zoning district adds a supplemental layer of regulations (such as historic preservation standards, floodplain restrictions, or airport-compatibility limits) on top of the underlying base zoning district, without replacing that district's base use and dimensional standards.
source_note: Standard national zoning law terminology -- overlay district, well-corroborated

question: A zoning ordinance that limits the total square footage of a building relative to the size of its lot (for example, a ratio of 2.0 permits a building with total floor area up to twice the lot area, potentially across multiple stories) is regulating:
choice_a: Floor Area Ratio (FAR)
choice_b: Setback distance
choice_c: Legal description
explanation: Floor Area Ratio (FAR) is a zoning density control expressed as the ratio of a building's total floor area to the area of the lot on which it sits; a FAR of 2.0 on a 10,000-square-foot lot would allow up to 20,000 square feet of total floor area, which could be distributed across multiple stories, distinguishing it from dimensional controls like setbacks or height limits.
source_note: Standard national zoning law terminology -- FAR, well-corroborated

question: The primary purpose of a zoning setback requirement -- a minimum distance a structure must be located from a lot line -- is generally to:
choice_a: Provide light, air, privacy, fire separation, and open space between structures and property lines
choice_b: Guarantee the property owner a specific resale price
choice_c: Determine the property's ad valorem tax assessment
choice_d: Establish the boundaries of the legal description in the deed
explanation: Zoning setback requirements establish minimum distances between structures and lot lines (front, side, and rear) primarily to ensure adequate light, air circulation, privacy, fire separation between buildings, and open space -- they are a dimensional zoning control, not a tax, valuation, or title/legal-description matter.
source_note: Standard national zoning law terminology -- setbacks, well-corroborated

question: A subdivision design technique that concentrates residential lots on a smaller portion of a tract at higher density while permanently preserving the remaining land as open space or agricultural land, rather than spreading development evenly across the entire parcel, is known as:
choice_a: Cluster (conservation) development
choice_b: Spot zoning
choice_c: Strip commercial zoning
explanation: Cluster development (also called conservation subdivision design) groups permitted residential units more closely together on a portion of a site, allowing the remaining acreage to be preserved as open space, agricultural land, or conservation area, while typically keeping the same overall density permitted for the tract as a whole.
source_note: Standard national zoning/planning law terminology -- cluster development, well-corroborated

question: A growth management tool that allows an owner of land with development potential that a jurisdiction wants to preserve (such as farmland or environmentally sensitive land) to sell that unused development potential to an owner of land in a designated growth area, who can then build at higher density than would otherwise be allowed, is called:
choice_a: Transfer of Development Rights (TDR)
choice_b: Eminent domain
choice_c: Adverse possession
explanation: Transfer of Development Rights (TDR) is a land use planning tool that severs the unused development potential from a 'sending' parcel (often one targeted for preservation, such as farmland, wetlands, or historic property) and allows it to be sold and used to increase density on a 'receiving' parcel located in an area the jurisdiction has designated for growth.
source_note: Standard national zoning/planning law terminology -- TDR, well-corroborated

question: A local government's temporary suspension of new development approvals or building permits within all or part of its jurisdiction, often adopted while it studies and updates its infrastructure capacity, zoning, or comprehensive plan, is called a:
choice_a: Development moratorium
choice_b: Variance
choice_c: Deed restriction
explanation: A development moratorium is a temporary, generally applicable halt on new development approvals or permit issuance, typically imposed while a local government addresses a specific problem such as inadequate infrastructure capacity or an outdated comprehensive plan; because it is temporary and general (not targeted at one parcel), it is treated differently under takings law than a permanent, parcel-specific restriction.
source_note: Standard national zoning/planning law terminology -- development moratorium, well-corroborated

question: Under the doctrine of vested rights, a developer who has obtained required approvals and made substantial, good-faith expenditures in reasonable reliance on existing zoning or land development regulations generally:
choice_a: May proceed with the approved project even if the zoning or regulations are later changed to prohibit it
choice_b: Must immediately halt all work the moment any zoning amendment is proposed
choice_c: Loses all rights in the project automatically upon any regulatory change
choice_d: Has no protection whatsoever against subsequent regulatory changes
explanation: The vested rights doctrine protects a developer who has obtained the necessary governmental approvals and made substantial good-faith expenditures or undertaken substantial construction in reasonable reliance on then-existing regulations, allowing the project to proceed to completion even if the zoning or land development regulations are subsequently changed to prohibit it.
source_note: Standard national zoning/planning law doctrine -- vested rights, well-corroborated

question: A developer whose proposed project already conforms to the applicable zoning classification and comprehensive plan designation, but who must still submit engineering, landscaping, drainage, and building layout details for staff-level administrative approval before a permit issues, is going through:
choice_a: Site plan review
choice_b: A rezoning hearing
choice_c: A comprehensive plan amendment
explanation: Site plan review is an administrative (typically staff-level, sometimes with public hearing) process that evaluates the detailed design of a development -- such as building placement, parking, drainage, landscaping, and access -- for compliance with existing land development regulations, and is distinct from a rezoning or comprehensive plan amendment, which changes the underlying land use entitlement itself.
source_note: Standard national zoning/planning law terminology -- site plan review, well-corroborated

question: The map component of a Florida local government's comprehensive plan that designates the proposed distribution, location, and density/intensity of land uses (residential, commercial, industrial, conservation, etc.) throughout the jurisdiction is the:
choice_a: Future Land Use Map (FLUM)
choice_b: Metes and bounds survey
choice_c: Plat of subdivision
explanation: The Future Land Use Map (FLUM) is the graphic component of a local government's comprehensive plan, required under Chapter 163, F.S., depicting the general distribution, location, and density or intensity of future land uses across the jurisdiction; local zoning maps and land development regulations must be consistent with the FLUM.
source_note: Section 163.3177, F.S. (comprehensive plan Future Land Use Element/Map requirement)

question: Florida's 'concurrency' requirement, implemented through local comprehensive plans under Chapter 163, F.S., generally requires that:
choice_a: Necessary public facilities and services (such as roads, water, sewer, and drainage) be available at the adopted level of service concurrent with the impacts of new development
choice_b: All new development be approved regardless of available infrastructure capacity
choice_c: Public transit facilities alone must meet concurrency, with no other public facility type included
choice_d: Only school concurrency applies, with no other public facility subject to the requirement
explanation: Concurrency, under Section 163.3180, F.S., requires that adequate public facilities and services needed to support development -- historically including roads/transportation, sanitary sewer, solid waste, drainage, potable water, and (where adopted) parks and schools -- be available concurrent with the impacts of that development, generally in place or under an enforceable commitment no later than issuance of a certificate of occupancy; public transit facilities are specifically exempted from the concurrency requirement.
source_note: Section 163.3180, F.S. (concurrency)

question: Under Florida's Community Planning Act, a local government's zoning ordinances and other land development regulations must be:
choice_a: Consistent with the adopted comprehensive plan
choice_b: Adopted independently of the comprehensive plan, with no required relationship between the two
choice_c: Approved by the Governor before taking effect
choice_d: Limited exclusively to residential land uses
explanation: Chapter 163, F.S. requires that land development regulations, including zoning ordinances, be consistent with the local government's adopted comprehensive plan -- the comprehensive plan functions as the overarching policy document, and zoning is the implementing regulatory tool that must conform to it, not an independent or freestanding system.
source_note: Section 163.3194, F.S. (legal status of comprehensive plan; consistency requirement)

question: A proposed amendment to a Florida local government's comprehensive plan Future Land Use Map affecting a large area or triggering statutory review thresholds generally follows the:
choice_a: State coordinated or expedited state review process, which involves review and comment from the state land planning agency and other reviewing entities before local adoption
choice_b: Same simplified process used for issuing an individual building permit
choice_c: No review process at all, since comprehensive plan amendments are self-executing
choice_d: Review exclusively by the Florida Real Estate Commission (FREC)
explanation: Large-scale comprehensive plan amendments in Florida go through the state coordinated review (or, for smaller/eligible amendments, expedited state) process under Section 163.3184, F.S., which includes transmittal to the state land planning agency (FloridaCommerce) and other reviewing agencies for comment before the local government holds an adoption hearing -- a distinct and more involved track than routine, staff-level regulatory approvals.
source_note: Section 163.3184, F.S. (process for adoption of comprehensive plan or plan amendment)

question: A Florida county or municipality that wants to use tax increment financing to rehabilitate a designated slum or blighted area may establish a Community Redevelopment Agency (CRA) under:
choice_a: Chapter 163, Part III, F.S. (the Community Redevelopment Act)
choice_b: Chapter 475, Part I, F.S.
choice_c: Chapter 720, F.S.
explanation: Chapter 163, Part III, F.S. (the Community Redevelopment Act) authorizes a local government to create a Community Redevelopment Agency after making a formal 'Finding of Necessity' that a designated area suffers from slum or blighted conditions, enabling tools such as tax increment financing to fund redevelopment within that area.
source_note: Sections 163.330-163.463, F.S. (Community Redevelopment Act)

question: Under the Florida Impact Fee Act, a local government imposing an impact fee on new construction to fund infrastructure such as roads, schools, or parks must ensure the fee is:
choice_a: Proportional to, and has a rational nexus with, the need for additional capital facilities generated by the new development
choice_b: Set at whatever amount the local government chooses, with no connection to the development's actual impact required
choice_c: Collected only after the certificate of occupancy is issued, never at or before the building permit stage
choice_d: Applicable exclusively to commercial development, never to residential construction
explanation: Section 163.31801, F.S. (the Florida Impact Fee Act) requires that an impact fee be proportional and reasonably connected to -- have a rational nexus with -- the need for additional capital facilities and the increased impact generated by the new residential or commercial construction, places the burden of proving this on the government in any legal challenge, and prohibits requiring collection earlier than issuance of the building permit for the property being charged.
source_note: Section 163.31801, F.S. (Florida Impact Fee Act)

question: Florida's designation of an 'Area of Critical State Concern' under Chapter 380, F.S. -- a designation applied to areas such as the Florida Keys, Big Cypress, the Green Swamp, and Apalachicola Bay -- reflects that the area contains:
choice_a: Environmental, historical, or natural resources of regional or statewide significance warranting heightened state oversight of local land use decisions
choice_b: No resources of any particular significance, the designation being purely honorary
choice_c: Property that is automatically exempt from all local zoning regulation
choice_d: Land that has been permanently withdrawn from private ownership
explanation: Under Section 380.05, F.S., the state may designate an Area of Critical State Concern where the area contains, or has a significant impact upon, environmental, historical, natural, or archaeological resources of regional or statewide importance -- examples include the Florida Keys, the Big Cypress Area, the Green Swamp, and the Apalachicola Bay Area -- triggering additional state-level review of local land use and development regulations within the designated area.
source_note: Section 380.05, F.S. (areas of critical state concern)

question: Historically under Florida's Chapter 380, a proposed development large enough to create impacts extending beyond the boundaries of a single local government (such as a very large mixed-use or resort project) could be reviewed as a:
choice_a: Development of Regional Impact (DRI)
choice_b: Special exception
choice_c: Homestead property
explanation: Under Chapter 380, F.S., a Development of Regional Impact (DRI) was a development of a scale determined likely to have substantial effects on more than one county, historically subject to a multi-agency review process involving the regional planning council and the state land planning agency in addition to the local government; 2015-2018 legislative changes eliminated new DRI review and the state/regional review of amendments to existing DRIs, though many previously approved DRIs remain vested and subject to their existing development orders.
source_note: Chapter 380, F.S.; Chapter 2018-158, Laws of Florida (eliminating state/regional DRI amendment review, effective April 9, 2018)

question: The Coastal Construction Control Line (CCCL), established by the Florida Department of Environmental Protection under Section 161.053, F.S., functions as:
choice_a: A jurisdictional line landward of which DEP does not require a state permit for construction, with a state permit generally required for construction or excavation activities seaward of the line
choice_b: A strict setback line beyond which no construction of any kind may ever occur, functioning identically everywhere along Florida's coast
choice_c: A boundary that determines property tax assessment values only
choice_d: A line used solely to mark county boundaries along the coast
explanation: The CCCL is a line of DEP jurisdiction, not a uniform construction setback line -- unless exempt, a state permit is required from DEP for construction, excavation, and dune vegetation removal activities seaward of the CCCL, in order to apply special siting and design standards protecting the beach-dune system, upland structures, and public beach access, while construction landward of the line generally falls outside CCCL permitting.
source_note: Section 161.053, F.S. (coastal construction control line); Florida DEP CCCL program materials

question: A property listed for sale is located seaward of Florida's Coastal Construction Control Line. A real estate licensee should understand that any proposed new construction, major renovation, or excavation on that property will likely require:
choice_a: A CCCL permit from the Florida Department of Environmental Protection, in addition to any local building permits
choice_b: No additional permitting beyond a standard local building permit
choice_c: Approval from FREC before construction may begin
explanation: Construction, excavation, or dune vegetation removal seaward of the CCCL generally requires a separate state CCCL permit from the Florida Department of Environmental Protection -- addressing coastal erosion, dune stability, and structure siting -- in addition to, not instead of, the local government building permit process.
source_note: Section 161.053, F.S.; Florida DEP CCCL permitting program

question: Florida's consolidated state permitting program that regulates activities affecting wetlands, surface water flows, stormwater management, and dredge-and-fill work -- administered jointly by the Florida DEP and the regional water management districts -- is known as the:
choice_a: Environmental Resource Permit (ERP) program
choice_b: Homeowners' association covenant enforcement program
choice_c: Real Estate Recovery Fund
explanation: Florida's Environmental Resource Permit (ERP) program consolidates state regulation of activities affecting wetlands, surface waters, and stormwater management -- including dredge-and-fill activity -- and is jointly administered by the Florida Department of Environmental Protection and the state's regional water management districts, operating alongside (not in place of) federal Clean Water Act Section 404 permitting by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers.
source_note: Florida DEP Environmental Resource Permitting (ERP) program; Chapter 373, F.S.

question: Florida's five regional water management districts (including the South Florida, Southwest Florida, St. Johns River, Suwannee River, and Northwest Florida districts) were established under Chapter 373, F.S. primarily to:
choice_a: Manage and regulate the state's water resources, including water supply, flood protection, water quality, and natural systems
choice_b: License and discipline real estate brokers and sales associates
choice_c: Administer the state's ad valorem property tax system
explanation: Florida's five water management districts, created under Chapter 373, F.S., are regional agencies (each governed by a gubernatorially appointed board) responsible for managing water resources within their boundaries, including water supply planning, flood protection and floodplain management, water quality monitoring, and regulatory permitting (such as consumptive use permits and environmental resource permits) affecting wetlands and surface waters.
source_note: Chapter 373, F.S. (water resources); Florida's five water management districts, well-corroborated

question: A waterfront property owner wants to build a private dock extending over state-owned submerged land. Because sovereign submerged lands in Florida are held in trust for the public, this typically requires:
choice_a: A submerged land lease or consent of use from the Board of Trustees of the Internal Improvement Trust Fund (or its delegated agency), in addition to any environmental permit
choice_b: No authorization of any kind, since riparian owners automatically own the submerged land beneath navigable water
choice_c: Approval from the county property appraiser only
explanation: Sovereign submerged lands beneath Florida's navigable waters are held in the public trust by the Board of Trustees of the Internal Improvement Trust Fund; while upland riparian owners generally have certain riparian rights (such as reasonable access to the water), structures like docks extending over sovereign submerged land typically require separate authorization (a lease, easement, or consent of use) from the state, in addition to any required environmental resource permit.
source_note: Chapter 253, F.S. (state lands); Florida sovereign submerged lands program, well-corroborated

question: Effective under Section 689.302, F.S., a seller of Florida residential real property must generally provide a prospective buyer with:
choice_a: A standalone flood disclosure, delivered at or before the contract is executed, addressing matters such as flood insurance coverage, past flood insurance claims, and known prior flood damage
choice_b: No flood-related disclosure of any kind, since flood risk in Florida is addressed solely through federal law
choice_c: A disclosure limited exclusively to commercial properties, never residential property
choice_d: A verbal-only statement about flood history, with no written form required
explanation: Section 689.302, F.S., enacted in 2024 and expanded effective October 1, 2025, requires that sellers of most Florida residential real property (including houses, condominiums, and manufactured homes) provide a separate, standalone written flood disclosure at or before contract execution, covering matters such as flood insurance, federal flood assistance received, and the seller's knowledge of flooding or flood damage during their ownership.
source_note: Section 689.302, F.S. (residential real property flood disclosure)

question: A home is located within a FEMA-designated Special Flood Hazard Area (SFHA), also referred to as a 100-year floodplain. A buyer obtaining a federally backed mortgage on this property will generally be required to:
choice_a: Purchase and maintain flood insurance for the life of the loan as a lender condition
choice_b: Forgo flood insurance entirely, since federally backed loans are exempt from any flood insurance requirement
choice_c: Obtain flood insurance only if the home has flooded in the past
choice_d: Rely on the seller to maintain flood insurance after closing
explanation: Under the National Flood Insurance Program, a lender making a federally backed or federally regulated mortgage loan on improved real property located in a FEMA-designated Special Flood Hazard Area must, as a condition of the loan, require the borrower to purchase and maintain flood insurance for the life of the loan.
source_note: National Flood Insurance Act / Flood Disaster Protection Act (federal mandatory flood insurance purchase requirement); general federal law, well-corroborated

question: A Florida local government's comprehensive plan includes a Coastal Management Element that limits residential density within the designated Coastal High Hazard Area (CHHA). The primary purpose of this density limitation is to:
choice_a: Reduce the population that must be evacuated from the highest-risk hurricane storm surge zone, easing hurricane evacuation and public safety
choice_b: Maximize property tax revenue collected from beachfront property
choice_c: Guarantee waterfront property owners an unobstructed view
choice_d: Ensure that all new coastal construction is exempt from building codes
explanation: Florida's Community Planning Act requires coastal comprehensive plans to address hurricane evacuation and limit development density within the Coastal High Hazard Area -- generally defined as the area below the Category 1 hurricane storm surge line -- primarily to reduce the population exposed to the highest storm surge risk and to keep hurricane evacuation times and clearance manageable.
source_note: Section 163.3178, F.S. (coastal management element; coastal high hazard area)

question: Florida's Bert J. Harris, Jr., Private Property Rights Protection Act allows a property owner to seek monetary compensation from a governmental entity when a new law, rule, or ordinance, as applied, has:
choice_a: Inordinately burdened an existing use of the real property or a vested right to a specific use, even though the action does not rise to the level of a formal taking
choice_b: Increased the property's fair market value
choice_c: Merely been proposed but never actually applied to the claimant's property
choice_d: Affected only a neighboring parcel, with no direct application to the claimant's own property
explanation: The Bert J. Harris, Jr., Private Property Rights Protection Act (Section 70.001, F.S.), enacted in 1995, provides a distinct state-law remedy allowing a property owner to seek compensation when a governmental regulation, as directly applied to the owner's specific property, inordinately burdens an existing use or a vested right to a specific use -- even where the burden falls short of a full taking under the state or federal constitution; a claim generally cannot be based on a regulation applied only to a neighboring property.
source_note: Section 70.001, F.S. (Bert J. Harris, Jr., Private Property Rights Protection Act)

question: Under Florida's Right to Farm Act, an established farm operation that has been in operation for one year or more and conforms to generally accepted agricultural practices is generally:
choice_a: Protected from being deemed a public or private nuisance solely because of encroaching residential or commercial development in a formerly rural area
choice_b: Required to cease operation the moment a new residential subdivision is approved nearby
choice_c: Automatically rezoned to residential use once surrounding development occurs
choice_d: Exempt from all state and federal environmental laws
explanation: The Florida Right to Farm Act (Section 823.14, F.S.) shields an established farm operation -- in place for at least one year and conforming to generally accepted agricultural and management practices -- from being found a public or private nuisance based on nuisance claims that arise as residential or commercial development encroaches on formerly rural, agricultural areas; it does not exempt the farm from state and federal environmental law compliance.
source_note: Section 823.14, F.S. (Florida Right to Farm Act)

question: A developer cannot avoid impacting a small area of jurisdictional wetlands and instead proposes to purchase credits from an approved offsite wetlands mitigation bank to compensate for the unavoidable loss. This approach reflects the general environmental permitting sequence of:
choice_a: Avoid and minimize wetland impacts first, then mitigate remaining unavoidable impacts, such as through an approved mitigation bank
choice_b: Mitigate first and avoidance/minimization is never considered
choice_c: Wetlands mitigation banks are prohibited under Florida and federal law
choice_d: Any wetland may be filled freely as long as the developer pays a fee afterward with no agency approval needed
explanation: Florida and federal wetlands permitting (under the state Environmental Resource Permit program and federal Clean Water Act Section 404 permitting) generally follow a sequence requiring an applicant to first avoid and then minimize wetland impacts, with compensatory mitigation -- such as purchasing credits from an agency-approved wetlands mitigation bank -- reserved for impacts that genuinely cannot be avoided or further minimized.
source_note: Florida DEP/water management district ERP mitigation requirements; federal Clean Water Act Section 404(b)(1) guidelines mitigation sequencing, well-corroborated

question: A proposed development requires a federal permit (such as a Clean Water Act Section 404 wetlands permit from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers) or federal funding. This federal involvement can trigger environmental review requirements under:
choice_a: The National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA)
choice_b: Chapter 475, F.S., Part I
choice_c: The Florida Real Estate Commission's licensing rules
explanation: The National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) requires federal agencies to evaluate the environmental effects of proposed major federal actions -- including projects requiring a federal permit (such as a Corps of Engineers Section 404 wetlands permit) or federal funding -- before proceeding, potentially requiring an environmental assessment or a more detailed environmental impact statement, separate from and in addition to state and local environmental review.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. Section 4321 et seq. (NEPA); general federal environmental law, well-corroborated

question: A local historic preservation ordinance designates a downtown building as a local historic landmark. As a practical matter for a broker listing that property, this designation typically means:
choice_a: Exterior alterations, demolition, or certain renovations will likely require review and a certificate of appropriateness from a historic preservation board, beyond the standard building permit process
choice_b: The property becomes automatically exempt from all local zoning and building codes
choice_c: The designation has no practical effect on how the property may be renovated or sold
choice_d: The property must be donated to the local government within one year
explanation: Local historic preservation designation (often implemented as an overlay district under local ordinance) typically requires that exterior alterations, demolition, or significant renovations to the designated structure be reviewed by a historic preservation board or similar body and receive a certificate of appropriateness, in addition to -- not instead of -- otherwise applicable building permits and zoning compliance, which brokers should disclose as a material use restriction to prospective buyers.
source_note: Standard national/Florida local historic preservation ordinance practice, well-corroborated
